newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines support EU on human rights deal.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines support EU on human rights deal.

text.p: Aborigines on Friday called on the European Commission to stand firm against Australia and not sign a trade treaty without a human rights clause.
"Just what is the Australian government trying to hide?" said Galarrwuy Yunupingu, chairman of the powerful Aboriginal Northern Land Council in the outback Northern Territory.
"The clause in question says both parties must respect democratic principles and basic human rights as proclaimed in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights," Yunupingu said.
"This is something the Australian government should be embracing, not rejecting," Yunupingu said in a statement.
Yunupingu countered Australia's argument that it opposed mixing trade and human rights, citing Australia's leading role in the sanctions campaign against apartheid South Africa.
The human rights clause, standard in EU agreements with other countries, allows the bloc to break off relations in the event of human rights abuses in that country.
It has led to protracted negotiations with other countries -- chiefly South Korea, Mexico and Turkey -- but is insisted upon by the European Parliament.
Yunupingu said the land council would send a dossier to the European Commission outlining Australia's poor track record on indigenous human rights.
Australia's 300,000 Aborigines are the country's most disadvantaged people. Aboriginal adults have a life expectancy 10 to 15 years lower than the rest of the 18 million population.
He said the document would include information on the government's plans to change native title land laws in favour of farmers -- a move that threatens to breach racial discrimination laws.
"The European Parliament should know that the Australian government is demonstrating scant regard for the human rights of indigenous Australians," Yunupingu said.
"The Australian government will happily trample over indigenous rights to enable the Australian pastoral and resource industries to get on with business at our expense."
The Australian government is under pressure from farmers, miners and conservative politicians to change native title laws to ensure pastoral leases dominate over native title rights.

The move follows a ruling by Australia's High Court in December allowing pastoral leases and native title to co-exist. Previously, pastoral leases extinguished native title rights, leaving Aborigines to claim only unoccupied crown land.

The judgment sent shudders through the farming and mining communities, as it leaves some 40 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) -- an area almost the size of India -- vulnerable to native title claim.
Farmers and miners warn the uncertainty of tenure will dry up investment in commodities -- the backbone of the Australian economy.
